subject: ventures/scale-reliability
professional: a psychometrician who reports scale reliability for questionnaire studies (checks first: is alpha/omega computed from the right matrix, is the Feldt interval on the right degrees of freedom, is omega a one-factor model-based omega total, are item-rest correlations corrected, and are the limits for ordinal data and multidimensionality stated)

evidence.correctness: Recomputed on the bundled PHQ-9 file (n=1494 complete, k=9) with my own numpy/scipy script (scratchpad/scalerel/recompute.py, textbook formulas, scipy 1.18.1, not the author's eval/reference.py): alpha 0.823622, Feldt 95% (0.809891, 0.836735) from scipy.stats.f, lambda-2 0.836544, lambda-6 0.826470 (via explicit OLS residual variances, not the inverse diagonal), ULS omega 0.838049 (scipy.optimize.least_squares on off-diagonal residuals, a third algorithm besides the engine's iterated principal axes and the author's BFGS), item-rest r for all 9 items, SEM 1.7292, Spearman-Brown 5/8/18 items, eigenvalues 3.845/0.982/0.819/0.715. Engine: identical to 1e-6 or better on every value. BCa alpha interval: engine (0.8059, 0.8413) vs scipy.stats.bootstrap method='BCa', 3000 resamples (0.8048, 0.8420), within Monte Carlo error. Edge probes run through cli.mjs: k=2, singular matrix (lambda-6 null with a warning), unreversed item (negative alpha with three warnings), reversal with --scale-min/max restores alpha 0.976, missing code 99 excluded before the reversal range. No wrong number found.
evidence.completeness: README/page/llms.txt features checked end to end: CLI text and --json (ran), stdin, --reverse/--scale-min/--scale-max/--missing/--confidence 0.9/--bootstrap (ran), platform/agents/tools.mjs call scale-reliability analyze (ran, returns result), identifier/text column skipping (ran: seqn skipped), warnings for negative items, Heywood, singular, small n, dropped rows (all observed), Spearman-Brown, omega if deleted, standardised omega, eigenvalues, BCa intervals. Page: served at https://marisstella.app/scale-reliability/ (HTTP 200, canonical rewritten correctly); its script imports the same engine.mjs; I did not drive the DOM in a browser, page.test.mjs covers ids, example and coverage table. No stubs or TODOs. Capped at 3 because the page was not driven interactively.
evidence.verification: node --test '*.test.mjs': 41/41 pass in 5.7 s. Tests check alpha/Feldt/loadings/lambdas against eval/reference.json (pingouin, factor_analyzer, scipy), plus properties (alpha<=lambda-2, invariances, simulated parallel items recover reliability, exact loadings recovery, reversal restores alpha, seeded bootstrap). Mutations via quality_mutate.py: Feldt df2 (n-1)(k-1)->(n-1)k caught; reliability band 0.8->0.85 caught; BCa acceleration divisor 6->3 SURVIVED (the only BCa test compares to the percentile interval at 0.01 on a large sample where acceleration is negligible); Spearman-Brown ceil->round SURVIVED (the only test uses an exact-integer case). 2 of 4 survived, both in reported outputs, so 3 not 4.
evidence.craft: Read engine.mjs (573 lines, pure functions, own Jacobi eigen, Gauss-Jordan, incomplete beta/gamma, BCa with jackknife downdating and duplicate-row caching), cli.mjs, eval/coverage.mjs, eval/reference.py, index.html script, data/SOURCE.md. Clean and well commented. Small issues: parseCsv computes the delimiter sort twice (engine.mjs:284) and prepare's find() calls findIndex twice (engine.mjs:326); eval/coverage.mjs:10-11 takes Number(argv) with no check, so `node eval/coverage.mjs --help` ran 0 reps and silently overwrote eval/coverage.json and coverage-data.mjs (the page's table) with nulls (I restored both with git checkout); a semicolon CSV with decimal commas gets the generic 'need at least two numeric item columns' error.
evidence.claims: Checked: alpha, Feldt and loadings 'checked against pingouin and factor_analyzer' (eval/reference.json present, tests compare to it; my own recomputation agrees); README example numbers alpha 0.824 (0.810-0.837), omega 0.838, lambda-2 0.837, self-harm item-rest 0.32, mean 0.04 (all reproduced by cli.mjs); coverage table in README equals eval/coverage.json row by row; page coverage prose (91-95%, 93/73/11%, 93-95%) matches the json after rounding; 'nothing is uploaded' (page script has no fetch; usage.mjs local counters with opt-out); disclaimer on page, README, CLI help and llms.txt; data provenance with SHA-256 in data/SOURCE.md. One small drift: README.md:82 says every equal-loading interval is 'within about 4 points of 95%' but BCa omega at n=200 is 90.7% (4.3 points). Not-modelled list (ordinal, multi-factor omega, GLB, weights) stated on README.
evidence.fitness: Job walked: a researcher pastes a 5-point Likert survey with two reverse-keyed items and a 99 missing code, sets scale range and reverse list, gets alpha with Feldt and BCa intervals, omega with BCa, item table with item-rest and if-deleted columns, warnings, and a JSON report; that is the reliability section of a methods paper. Gaps a psychometrician would hit: no ordinal (polychoric) alpha/omega for 4-point items like the bundled PHQ-9, only listwise deletion (no pairwise/FIML), no hierarchical omega for multi-subscale instruments, no Duhachek/Hakstian-Whalen alternative alpha intervals. All are stated limits.
evidence.domain: Compared against Cronbach 1951, Feldt et al. 1987 (df n-1 and (n-1)(k-1), correct), McDonald 1999 omega total with model-implied denominator (psych's observed-denominator variant also exported), Guttman 1945 lambda-2/6 definitions, Kelley & Pornprasertmanit 2016 (BCa for omega, which their coverage simulation corroborates: 93-95% vs alpha's 11% at n=1000 under congeneric loadings), Efron 1987 BCa (z0 and acceleration formulas correct). Departures are documented: ULS not ML for omega, lambda-6 on covariances not correlations, Pearson not polychoric. The example data are heavily floored 0-3 items where an ordinal coefficient would be the senior choice; the page does not nudge the user toward that.

defects.what: The BCa acceleration is not pinned by any test: doubling it (divisor 6 -> 3) leaves all 41 tests green, because the only BCa test compares to the percentile interval at tolerance 0.01 on n=1494, where acceleration is negligible. A small-n skewed case checked against scipy.stats.bootstrap(method='BCa') or a hand jackknife would catch it.
Spearman-Brown item count rounding is untested beyond an exact-integer case: ceil -> round survives (on the example it would report 17 items for 0.9 instead of 18).

eval/coverage.mjs converts argv with Number() and no check, so a non-numeric argument (e.g. --help) runs 0 replications and silently overwrites eval/coverage.json and coverage-data.mjs (the page's coverage table) with nulls.

A semicolon-delimited CSV with decimal commas (European export) makes every column non-numeric and gets the generic 'need at least two numeric item columns' error, without naming the decimal-comma cause.
README says every equal-loading interval is 'within about 4 points of 95%'; eval/coverage.json has BCa omega at n=200 at 90.7% (4.3 points). The page's 'about 91 to 95%' is accurate.

verdict: A correct, well-documented internal-consistency tool. Every number I recomputed independently on the bundled NHANES PHQ-9 data (alpha, Feldt CI, lambda-2, lambda-6 by a different route, ULS omega by a third optimiser, item-rest r, SEM, Spearman-Brown, BCa alpha vs scipy) agreed to 1e-6 or within bootstrap noise, and the README/page claims, coverage table and provenance are backed by files. It meets the bar. Its gaps are in verification (BCa acceleration and Spearman-Brown rounding mutants survive) and the stated method limits a psychometrician would still want for ordinal Likert data (no polychoric coefficients, listwise deletion only, no hierarchical omega). The worst defect is the untested BCa acceleration (medium); the rest are low.
